scenario.name: Kaspersky GReAT — Operation Triangulation: Zero-Click Font Exploit, MMIO & TriangleDB
scenario.shortSubtitle: Kaspersky Securelist · CVE-2023-41990 ADJUST TrueType Font, CVE-2023-38606 MMIO & TriangleDB
scenario.overview: Imagine a pocket fortress smartphone locked behind custom hardware walls that even master locksmiths cannot read from public manuals. An invisible message arrives silently with zero taps needed, triggering a microscopic drawing-font glitch inside a hidden attachment; the hidden intruder then unlocks an undocumented secret hardware dial built straight into the phone's silicon chip to rewrite protected rooms, erases the delivery message without a trace, and lives purely inside temporary working memory until the phone restarts. In this scenario (CVE-2023-41990, Kaspersky GReAT, Operation Triangulation: Zero-Click Font Exploit, MMIO & TriangleDB), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: zero-Click iMessage Attachment Triggers, then bypassing Hardware Memory Protection, then deleting Message Traces. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Zero-Click iMessage Attachment Triggers, then Bypassing Hardware Memory Protection, then Deleting Message Traces, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: ZERO-CLICK IMESSAGE TRUETYPE ADJUST EXPLOIT (CVE-2023-41990)
stages.subtitle: Undocumented TrueType font opcode 0x8F/0x90 triggers JOP inside IMTransferAgent
stages.description: Without the phone owner ever clicking a link or even seeing a notification chime, a hidden message attachment feeds a warped drawing instruction into the phone's font renderer, quietly seizing control inside the messaging background clerk. The target iPhone receives an iMessage containing a disguised PDF/archive attachment with an embedded TrueType font. Even while the phone is locked in a pocket, the background daemon IMAgent (the iOS process that automatically pre-processes incoming iMessage attachments before showing a notification) parses the font using libFontParser.dylib. Inside the font, an obsolete 1990s TrueType bytecode instruction named ADJUST (opcode 0x8F/0x90, CVE-2023-41990) triggers an out-of-bounds memory write, giving the attacker instant code execution inside IMAgent with zero user clicks ("Zero-Click"). TrueType fonts are not just static shapes; they contain a Turing-complete virtual machine (font hinting bytecode) designed in the early 1990s. Abusing the legacy ADJUST instruction corrupts the C++ vtable on the heap inside IMAgent before any UI notification is ever rendered. Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ IMTRANSFERAGENT C2 / ⇠#1 RESP TLS 1.3) from Node ① (#1 Triangulation Validator & C2) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky triangle_check & NDR).

stages.title: XNU INTEGER OVERFLOW & HARDWARE MMIO BYPASS (CVE-2023-38606)
stages.subtitle: Bypassing hardware Page Protection Layer (PPL) via undocumented SoC MMIO registers
stages.description: Facing silicon-level armor designed to stop even a hijacked building manager from rewriting locked guard vaults, the intruder speaks directly to an undocumented secret hardware dial hidden inside the phone's silicon chip to slip straight around the memory shield. Even after escalating into the iOS kernel, Apple Silicon chips enforce a hardware-backed Page Protection Layer (PPL, which blocks even the operating system kernel itself from modifying protected user-signing tables or injecting unsigned code). To bypass PPL, the exploit writes directly to undocumented physical Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO) hardware registers at address 0x206040000 (CVE-2023-38606, an unmapped hardware debugging/DMA block built into the Apple A12–A16 System-on-Chip). By commanding this hardware DMA engine to write directly to physical RAM, the attacker overwrites PPL-protected kernel memory completely outside the CPU’s security checks. Because the CPU’s MMU/PPL checks only apply to memory writes executed by the CPU cores themselves, instructing an on-chip peripheral DMA engine via MMIO registers to write to physical memory bypasses PPL page-table write protection. In the documented CVE-2023-38606 MMIO exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC), IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC) responds with ALERT Ring-0 / PPL (confirming that the MMIO DMA PPL BYPASS request succeeded on IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 IN-MEMORY TRIANGLEDB IMPLANT DEPLOYMENT). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ MMIO DMA PPL BYPASS / ⇠#2 ALERT Ring-0 / PPL) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky triangle_check & NDR).

stages.title: IN-MEMORY TRIANGLEDB IMPLANT DEPLOYMENT
stages.subtitle: Loading memory-only Mach-O implant (CRConfig, CROs, CRAudio)
stages.description: Sweeping away the original message envelope so the phone chat history looks completely untouched, the spy deploys a purely memory-resident listening post that records microphone audio, location, and keychain secrets until a reboot wipes RAM clean. With full kernel privileges, the exploit first deletes the triggering iMessage record from sms.db and attachment caches (so the victim never sees an unread message and forensic investigators cannot extract the exploit file from the phone), then launches the TriangleDB spyware implant strictly in volatile RAM (meaning zero implant files are written to flash storage; if the phone is rebooted, the implant vanishes completely to avoid capture) while beaconing to 198.51.100.201:443. Even though TriangleDB deletes its iMessage entry and runs only in RAM, iOS automatically records how many bytes of cellular/Wi-Fi data each process uses inside DataUsage.sqlite, leaving orphaned network-usage rows and timestamp gaps that Kaspersky’s triangle_check forensic tool uses to prove infection. In the documented Mach-O TriangleDB exchange from IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC) to XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers, XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers responds with ALERT 220 KB Mach-O (confirming that the LOAD TRIANGLEDB request succeeded on XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers and completing the final execution objective of Kaspersky GReAT, Operation Triangulation: Zero-Click Font Exploit, MMIO & TriangleDB). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ LOAD TRIANGLEDB / ⇠#3 ALERT 220 KB Mach-O) from Node ③ (#3 IMTransferAgent (Font & JSC)) to Node ④ (#4 XNU Kernel & MMIO DMA Registers), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Kaspersky triangle_check & NDR).

detectionRule.title: Kaspersky GReAT — Operation Triangulation MMIO Kernel Exploit
detectionRule.ruleCode:
rule Kaspersky_OperationTriangulation_MMIO_Exploit {
  meta:
    author = "Kaspersky GReAT"
    cve = "CVE-2023-38606 / CVE-2023-32434"
  strings:
    $s1 = "/private/var/mobile/Library/SMS/sms.db" ascii
    $s2 = "IMTransferAgent" ascii
    $mmio = { 00 00 04 06 02 00 00 00 }
  condition:
    uint32(0) == 0xFEEDFACF and 2 of them
}
detectionRule.mitigation: Inspect iTunes backups using Kaspersky triangle_check for modified Info.plist/Manifest.db timestamps coinciding with IMTransferAgent network activity.

detectionRule.title: Kaspersky GReAT Official YARA — TriangleDB Spyware Implant
detectionRule.ruleCode:
rule Kaspersky_APT_OperationTriangulation_TriangleDB {
  meta:
    author = "Kaspersky GReAT (Securelist)"
    reference = "Dissecting TriangleDB"
  strings:
    $c1 = "CRConfig" ascii
    $c2 = "CRPoller" ascii
    $c3 = "CROs" ascii
    $c4 = "CRAudio" ascii
    $c5 = "populateWithFields" ascii
  condition:
    uint32(0) == 0xFEEDFACF and 4 of ($c*)
}
detectionRule.mitigation: Rebooting the device purges the memory-resident TriangleDB implant; block the C2 domains at the DNS/firewall layer and patch to the latest OS release.
